Ei vero dura proposita sunt, quae formidat caro, ad quae contremiscit; sed ad haec spiritus Dei munere roboratur, accingitur, leve reputans omne quod patitur, dum de retributionis suae munere gloriatur. Quod quidem audiens Synagoga, stat, stupet, et contremiscit, et in se tandem reversa, ait, « Nescivi, » id est, tantam gratiam et dona spiritus tibi collata ignoravi; ideoque, « anima mea conturbavit me, » quia in tenebris aberravi, « propter quadrigas Aminadab. » Aminadab iste Judae abnepos fuisse legitur [n: (I Par. II, 10)], qui sui nominis interpretatione, Christum significat; Aminadab [1288A] enim, « Spontaneus populi mei, » interpretatur; ipse enim totius populi caput exstitit, in cujus ortu Angelus ad pastores ait: « Nolite timere; ecce enim evangelizo vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo: quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus [n: (Luc. II, 10, 11)]. » Iste vero spontaneus ejus exstitit; sponte enim natus, sponte per angelos et virtutibus magnis demonstratus, sponte miraculis decoratus, sponte traditus, sponte in mortem datus; quae cum omnia sponte pertulerit, recte et populi, et ejus spontaneus, nominatur. Cujus quidem quadrigae, sunt quatuor Evangelia, quae per mundum trahuntur, dum praedicantur populis, et creduntur, et omni veneratione digna suscipiuntur. Quod contemplans [1288B] Synagoga, conturbatur, falsum esse desperans quod sic a cunctis corde suscipitur, magnifice honoratur, quod nec exquisitis tormentis, nec aliquo genere mortis eliditur. Sanctus vero Ambrosius duas denotat quadrigas. Iram enim, cupiditatem, voluptatem, et timorem unius quadrigae rotas facit; alteri vero prudentiam, temperantiam, fortitudinem, et justitiam assignat: his rotis tunc vitae spiritus inest, cum bonus eas rector dirigit, hos stringens, hos monens, hos revocans, hos incitans. Hi quidem equi subjecti jugo fidei, adstricti charitatis vinculo, justitiae fraenis, retinaculis sobrietatis. Sequitur:

12. *Revertere, revertere, Sulamitis: revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te.*

[1288C]Synagoga confitente tarditatem, Ecclesia consolando respondet, « Revertere, » etc. Dicitur Sulamiti ut revertatur, quia Synagogae in fine mundi fides ab Ecclesia offeretur, quae sub infidelitate captiva tenebatur. Et quater reverti monetur, quia Judaei per quatuor mundi partes dispersi, in fine colligentur; unde ei dicitur, « Revertere, revertere, Sulamitis, » quae captiva vel despecta sub prophetis tenebaris, « revertere, revertere, » ut in ea qua sumus libertate, « intueamur te. » Sequitur:



## CAPUT VII.

1. *Quid videbis in Sulamite, nisi choros castrorum?*

Vox Sponsi haec est. Ecce Ecclesia monente Synagogam, [1288D] Sponsus gaudens, dare se promittit effectum, dicens, « Quid videbis in Sulamite, nisi choros castrorum? » Chori namque castrorum sunt qui in procinctu virtutum tanquam in castris constituti, contra diabolum dimicant, et Deo muniente, et opem sua virtute ferente, superant. Tunc enim castra militantium in Sulamite videbuntur, quando pro fide, quam modo impugnat, praeliabitur, et eamdem praedicantibus Henoch et Elia, veram, et eam in qua salvari oporteat fore asserens, morte sua contestabitur. Sequitur:

2. *Quam pulchri sunt gressus tui in calceamentis, filia Principis!*

Laudat ecce Sponsus Sponsam, incipiens a gressibus: unde et hanc commendans, ait: « Quam [1289A] pulchri sunt gressus tui in calceamentis, filia Principis! » Hanc quidem quae in primis suis patribus « filia Principis, » id est, Dei super omnia principantis exstitit, duodena laude commendat, a gressibus incipiens, per media progrediens, et ejus laudem uberum foecunditate consummans; ait itaque, O quae nunc in conversatione tua filia vocari Principis digna es, quae etiam in primis tuis patribus, ejus dici filia digne promeruisti, « quam pulchri » nunc « sunt gressus tui! » Ad Deum enim nunc eisdem accedis gressibus, quibus apostoli accesserunt; Dei Filium, a Patre missum in carnem, ipsumque in eadem carne pro omnium salute mortem obiisse, et post triduum resurrexisse, et sic, habita victoria, in coelum ascendisse, confitens, pro illo stas, illi [1289B] testimonium perhibes, pro ipso mori non recusas. Valde ergo pulchri sunt gressus tui, quibus ad Deum ambulas; et hoc, « in calceamentis. » Fiunt namque calceamenta de coriis mortuorum animalium; unde per haec, exempla sanctorum intelliguntur: Patrum, apostolorum, scilicet, et omnium martyrum, quia coria sibi detrahi, et ab animabus corpora subtrahi, Christum confitendo, perpessi sunt. His igitur aequaris, his aequalis efficeris, qui, fide certa suscepta, pro ea dimicas, et apostolorum gloria coronari pro ea contendendo elaboras. Sequitur:

*Juncturae femorum tuorum sicut monilia, quae fabricata sunt manu artificis.*

[1289C]Femina vel femora quibus gradimur, et [cn: 69 | F. *gressus*.] egressus aptamus, haec duo sunt, Testamentum scilicet Vetus et Novum: horum junctura concordia Testamentorum est, de qua ait, « Junctura femorum tuorum sicut monilia. » Monilia quidem a monendo dicta sunt, eo quod ubi collo suspenduntur, et pectoribus apponuntur, monent quidem haec gerentem, ne ad sinum suum manum mittat alienam, sed ei cui desponsata est, fidem conservet intemeratam. Monent et quemlibet, ne ubi haec suspensa viderit, illuc amore trahatur, aut quocunque casu illuc amore rapiatur, ne forte deprehensus in hoc, adulterii reus habeatur. Unde duo Testamenta merito monilia nominantur, quae nos Deum timere monent, et venerari, et toto [1289D] corde, tota anima, et totis viribus hunc diligere, et mente firma meditari. Monent etiam, ut proximos diligamus, nec quicquam eis quod recte displicere debeat, machinemur aut faciamus. In his duo Testamenta sunt et concordant, quae etiam fidem, sicut vere est, sic roborant; et sicut credimus, sic esse confirmant. Haec etiam « manu artificis fabrefacta sunt, » id est, per Filium, qui manus Patris est, et summus omnium artifex, hominibus edicta sunt, atque conscripta. Sequitur:

3. *Umbilicus tuus crater tornatilis, nunquam indigens poculis.*

Umbilicus quidem in medio ventris est, quamdam [1290A] ejus partem subter se habens, quamdam vero desuper. Hic autem umbilicus infirmitas nostrae mortalitatis est, cujus pars quaedam deorsum est, altera vero desursum. Deorsum illa est, de qua dicitur: « Omnis caro foenum, et omnis gloria ejus quasi flos agri. Exsiccatum est foenum, et cecidit flos [n: (Isa. XL, 6, 7)]. » De qua ait David: « Mane sicut herba transeat, mane floreat, et transeat: vespere decidat, induret, et arescat [n: (Psal. LXXXIX, 6)]. » Transit etiam mane infantiae, pueritiae, adolescentiae nostrae; transit et flos juventutis nostrae, transit et [cn: 70 | F. *vesper*.] vespere senectutis nostrae: in quo quidem homo decidit in morte, indurat in cadavere, arescit in pulvere. Illa vero desursum est, cujus beatus Paulus meminit, dicens: « Seminatur in [1290B] corruptione, surget in incorruptione: seminatur in ignobilitate, surget in gloria: seminatur in infirmitate, surget in virtute: seminatur corpus animale, surget spirituale [n: (I Cor. XV, 42, 43)]. » Hic igitur umbilicus, ut crater tornatilis est: levissima enim operatio est quae torno fit; et levissima Dei operatio, quae in omnium fiet resurrectione. Nam ut Habacuc levissime levavit angelus, et posuit in Babylone; sic cibum Danieli deferens, ipsumque in Judaea reposuit [n: (Dan. XIV, 35)]: sic erit in resurrectione, cum ad vocem angeli, ad tubae clangentis sonitum, mortui resurgent illico incorrupti, qui quidem digni fuerunt corruptela. Haec itaque pars est infirmitatis nostrae quae torno operationis divinae leviter efficietur, quae crater dicitur tornatilis, qui [1290C] nec hic indiget poculis, nec in futuro aliquatenus indigebit. Hic igitur magna eorum gloria futura dicitur, quae tunc et corporaliter videbitur, et apparebit. Sequitur:

*Venter tuus sicut acervus tritici, vallatus liliis.*

Venter ea pars corporis est, quae quod in eam mittitur, id suscipit; et quod in ea potest cooperari substantiae, id retinet, eo corpus fovet, auget, et provehit, caetera repellit et respuit. Unde per hunc sancta hujus synagogae memoria intelligitur, quae comprehendit omnia, et haec tantum quae sancta sunt, et aeternae vitae cooperantia, illucque gressus dirigentia, haec amat, haec custodit, et in his proficit: caetera ut vana et inutilia respuit et [1290D] emittit. Unde et dicitur: « Venter tuus sicut acervus tritici. » In acervo namque tritici, vitae quaedam cooperantia sunt, quaedam aliter se habent: de his vero quae cooperantur ad vitam, subditur, quod acervus hic « vallatur liliis, » id est, Patrum eruditur exemplis, et coelestium spirituum, qui vere lilia sunt, edocetur documentis. Sequitur:

4. *Duo ubera tua, sicut duo hinnuli gemelli capreae. 5. Collum tuum sicut turris eburnea.*

Hoc de uberibus synagogae conversae, sicut et de uberibus Ecclesiae supra dictum est, intelligitur; sicut et quod de collo sequitur, « Collum tuum sicut turris eburnea: » hic tamen additur, « eburnea, » [1291A] ut et nitor demonstretur praedicationis, et firmitas, qua Christum vere praedicant, et hoc sua morte confirmant. Sequitur:

*Oculi tui sicut piscinae in Hesebon, quae sunt in porta filiae multitudinis.*

Demonstrato collo, pervenitur ad oculos; de quibus hic dicitur, quia ii sunt « sicut piscinae in Hesebon. » Hesebon vero, « cingulus moeroris, » interpretatur. « Oculi » vero, id est, qui arcana fidei contemplantur, et haec conversae jam synagogae videnda et credenda demonstrant, hi sunt « sicut piscinae in Hesebon: » Hesebon enim, sive castellum sit, sive civitas, in ipso suo introitu piscinas habebat, in quibus introeuntium corpora lavari poterant et purgari, ut sic fides haberetur ingressis, [1291B] se nil mali machinaturos, quod loco foret adversum, vel aliquatenus obfuturum. Sic et hi, qui conversae huic synagogae vias vitae praeparant, et ostendunt, aliis ad eam convertendis viam vitae praevident et ostendunt, et ut ficte non subeant, Baptismum vane non suscipiant, nec adversari machinentur in dolo his in quibus jam regnat Christus, atque suum jam continet principatum. Hoc igitur est quod dicitur, « quae sunt in porta filiae multitudinis, » id est, in ingressu castelli vel civitatis, ubi multitudo est gentium, cui jam praedicatur Dei verbum, et hoc suscipiunt in secula seculorum. Hoc enim Simon Magus ille ficte fecit, Baptismum ficte suscepit, fidei sacramenta ficte cognovit, quibus omnibus postea doctorem Ecclesiae Petrum a Christo institutum acriter [1291C] impugnavit. Unde ne hanc in conversione sua, cum haec dabitur, similis inquietet impugnatio, dicitur huic, quod ei erunt oculi praevidentes sibi, sicut in portis Hesebon praevidebatur civitati. Haec vero multitudo recte, « cingulus moeroris, » dicitur; quia undique moerore cincta est. Hinc se Deo peccasse luget, inde, ne peccet, item lacrymas timoris habet; hinc sibi quaeritur deesse quem diligit, et praemia sibi deesse quae quaerit et appetit. Hoc igitur moerore cincta, recte Hesebon dicitur, quae his et aliis, quae dat compunctio, lacrymis circumdata recte conqueritur. Sequitur:

*Nasus tuus sicut turris Libani, quae respicit contra Damascum.*

[1291D]Naso deputantur Ecclesiae, quae virtutum fragrantiam in Ecclesia prope sentiunt, et foetorem vitiorum in ea a longe discernendo cognoscunt. Hi in Libano, qui candorem Ecclesiae designat, velut turris existunt, qui in Ecclesia Dei prae aliis nomen praelationis officiumque suscipiunt, et in Damascum respiciunt. Damascus enim Syriae metropolis est, ubi Cain Abel interfecisse legitur; unde mala multa illata sunt Israeli, ubi regnat infidelitas, et peccatum valde grassatur. Contra hunc Ecclesia Dei valde respicit, attente considerans, si quis sit, quem sibi possit eripere, et ereptum diabolo, ad Christum queat convertere. Sequitur:

5. *Caput tuum ut Carmelus: et comae capitis tui sicut purpura Regis vincta canalibus.*



## CAPUT VII. (cont.)

[1292A]Carmelus mons est, in quo ascendens Elias pluviam septem annis clausam, sibi a Deo dari abundanter obtinuit, Christum certe significans, quem confitentes, et quae de eo dicuntur vera esse asserentes, oramus ad Patrem, ut nobis gratiarum suarum dona emittat, per quae suae nos placitos voluntati efficiat. Hic vero Carmelus, « mons, » sive, « scientia circumcisionis, » interpretatur; quod Christo recte competit; ipse enim circumcisionis initium et finis exstitit. Ipse enim hanc Abrahae (qui diem ejus vidit et gavisus est) et ejus domui injunxit, coitum sibi vetitum, et caetera quaeque inhonesta et superflua cujusque membri, membri hujus austera praecisione interdixit. Ipse quoque hanc suscepit in se, et hanc in se consummatam esse [1292B] praedixit: sanguinis enim ejus, tam in cruce, quam in hac circumcisione, effusio, populo gratiae sufficiens correctio est, ut a vitiis abstineant, motusque pravos, non illa austeritate sacramenti, sed fidei solius et sancti baptismatis susceptione corrigant et emendent. Hujus vero capitis comae sunt, de quibus subjungitur: « Comae capitis tui sicut purpura Regis vincta canalibus. » Comae quidem capitis sunt quae caput adornant, faciem decorant, et capiti semper inhaerentes, id multa sui specie obvianti cuilibet honorabile reddunt, et omni veneratione dignissimum. Per has quidem hos intelligimus, qui summo Regi Christo, indissolubili amoris vinculo toto corde inhaerentes, ab ipso nunquam dividi, nec principatu, nec aliqua id agente potestate, potuerunt; [1292C] sed per omnia, quae adinveniri poterant, tormenta, ipsi vere adhaerere, et dici comae inseparabiles meruerunt. Et comae quidem capitis, ut purpura Regis vincta canalibus. Canales quidem sunt emissiones gratiarum Dei, quas modis pluribus in suos quos eligit, ipsosque martyrii gratia dignos efficit ipse et suscipit. In his itaque canalibus hae comae sunt, et iis quidem conjunctae sunt, nescientes ab iis disjungi, sed magis in his accepto liquore aliquo coelesti, fiant ut purpura Regis vincta canalibus rubicunda, Christo quidem in cruce passo conformata, et ipsi jam conformes in gloria. Sequitur:

6. *Quam pulchra es et quam decora, charissima, [1292D] in deliciis!*

Post eorum commendationem quae dicta sunt, laudem subjungit synagogae, quae jam Ecclesia effecta est, dicens, Quando sic se habent quae jam dicta sunt, ergo valde « pulchra es » in virtutis opere, et « decora » in ejusdem contemplatione; chara nobis per conversionem, per virtutis executionem charior, Deo in perventione « charissima; » unde subdit, « in deliciis, » id est, in his quae dicta sunt, quae Deus perhibet esse delicias, et in his tanquam deliciis oblectatur. Sequitur:

7. *Statura tua assimilata est palmae, et ubera tua botris.*

Hujus incepit a gressibus commendatio; junctura quoque feminum, umbilicus, et venter commendata [1293A] sunt; ubera, et collum, nasus, oculique, cum capite, et comis, descripta sunt. Quod ne videatur absonum, ejusque staturae nimis in se contractae dissonum, adjicit de statura, dicens, quod haec assimilata est palmae, sursum, scilicet, porrecta, in imo stricta et aspera, in coelum brachiis expansa et dilatata, fructum faciens suavissimum, qui conjunctus botris qui vineae fructus est, coenam reddit opulentam, et ipsam fructu vineae jucundissimam. Sequitur:

8. *Dixi: Ascendam in palmam, et apprehendam fructus ejus: et erunt ubera tua sicut botri vineae, et odor oris tui sicut malorum.*

Hoc quidem Sponsus ait, quod ipse in palmam ascendet; quod quidem impletum fuisse credimus, [1293B] cum ipse lignum crucis ascendit. Cui quidem et hoc datum est, ut sicut ipse hanc ascendendo super omnia victor exstitit, ita et haec super omnia ligna sylvarum juste principatum obtinuit, et recte dici palma promeruit; unde et ei decantatur, super omnia ligna sylvarum, tu sola fuisti digna sustinere Regem seculorum et Dominum. « Et apprehendam fructus ejus. » Hic hujus palmae fructus exstitit, immortalitas, impassibilitas, aeterna quoque jucunditas: hos ejus fructus Christus in cruce percepit. Nam quia humiliavit se, factus in cruce obediens Patri usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, exaltavit illum Pater, ut in nomine ejus omne genu flectatur, coelestium, terrestrium, et infernorum, [1293C] et omnis lingua confiteatur, quod ipse est in gloria Patris, ad quam nisi per ipsum nemo pervenit. « Et erunt ubera tua sicut botri vineae. » Ubera sunt quibus parvulorum alitur et nutritur infantia; quae dicta sunt prophetarum, quibus longe ante temporibus passio Christi prophetata est, multisque eorundem praeconiis adnunciata. Quae quidem ubera nunc botri vineae effecta sunt, nunc ipsum fructum ostendentia quem prophetabant, tunc demum cum Christus in cruce passus est, effectum quem personabant demonstrantia. « Et odor oris tui sicut malorum. » Odor enim crucis, antequam eam Christus ascenderet, erat horribilis; sed postquam Christus vitae dator ascendit, odores ejus omnes suavissimi facti sunt, atque, ut malorum odores, gratissimi; [1293D] unde et Paulus ait: « Christi bonus odor sumus Deo in iis qui salvi fiunt, et in iis qui pereunt [n: (II Cor. II, 15)]. » Sequitur:

9. *Guttur tuum sicut vinum optimum, dignum Dilecto meo ad potandum, labiisque et dentibus illius ad ruminandum. Ego Dilecto meo, et ad me conversio ejus.*

Dignam laude jamdiu hanc commendavit Sponsus, ab imo incipiens et ad summa progrediens; quod gratum habens Sponsa respondet: « Guttur tuum sicut vinum optimum, dignum Dilecto meo ad potandum, labiisque et dentibus illius ad ruminandum. » Ostendit itaque laudem, quam de ea Sponsus ipse personuit, eam esse, quam dignum est ut ab ipso Sponso potetur, et in ejus corpus transjecta, [1294A] memoriter teneatur; et hoc est quod dicitur, « labiis et dentibus ruminandum. » In lege enim [n: (Levit. XI, 3)], animal quod non ruminat, immundum habetur, et hoc quod ruminat, mundum procul dubio reputatur: nam qui bona quae audit vel legit, ad memoriam revocat, et haec dentibus ruminando, vel labiis pronunciando, denunciat, mundum esse animal perhibetur. Unde et hanc munditiam Sponso inesse perhibens, hortatur ut laudem hanc ad memoriam revocet, et eam laude hac dignam deputet atque dijudicet. Quod quidem et futurum esse denunciat, dicens, « Ego dilecto meo, et ad me conversio ejus; » ac si dicat, Ego memoria Dilecti mei digna sum, et ipse, ut a me in memoria habeatur, dignissimus: ego enim Patrem diligo, unigenitum [1294B] ejus Filium veneror et adoro, his Spiritum Sanctum in omnibus aequalem judico. Patris opera, quae pro me redimendo gessit, intelligo; in his Filii obedientiam recognosco, et per advenientem in me ejus Spiritum, ipsum ad me conversum, ejusque dona suscipio. Ait itaque, Ego Dilecto meo digna et chara sum: ipse enim pro me exinanivit seipsum, puerum faciens et parvulum; cui decantat Ecclesia illud Isaiae: « Parvulus natus est nobis, et Filius datus est nobis [n: (Isai. IX, 6)]. » Exinanivit etiam se factus obediens Patri usque ad mortem; et quam mortem? eam quae crucis erat, quae indignissima putabatur, qua coelum homini negabatur, terra subtrahebatur, aquae remedium non praestabatur, [1294C] et extinctus in aere lacerandus avibus committebatur:

*His merito charus, meritis his charus habendus.*

« Ad me » quoque « ejus conversio » est: nam quod genus mortis exhorream, cum Dei Filium talia pro me passum intelligam? nullum equidem. In Stephano namque lapidem, in Jacobo gladium, Romae in beato Petro crucem, in ejus consorte beato Paulo gladii molesta, sustinui; fervens oleum in Joanne, in Andrea crucis amara, pertuli, et in apostolis, et in omnibus per mundum late martyribus, quae poterant excogitari tormenta, praesentavi. Sequitur:

10. *Veni, Dilecte mi, egrediamur in agrum.*

Demonstrata charitate qua Christo unitur Ecclesia, [1294D] ipsum secure invocat, optans, ut ad se diligentem ipse quoque veniat, et diligentem se conspiciat, et an vera sint quae de eo sunt dicta, perspiciat. Ait itaque, « Veni, Dilecte mi, » quem usque ad mortem diligo, qui Ecclesiae discedens promisisti, dicens: « Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem seculi. » [n: (Matth. XXVIII, 20.)] « Veni, egrediamur in agrum. » Campus locus est late patens, sylvas, et loca sylvis carentia continens, hinc spinis obsessus, inde loca non spinosa, sed tamen inculta demonstrans, mundum designans hunc, qualis fuit, cum in ipsum Adam post peccatum trajectus est, et est ei sententia dicta, « Quia comedisti de ligno, ex quo praeceperam tibi ne comederes, maledicta terra in opere tuo: in laboribus comedes ex ea cunctis [1295A] diebus vitae tuae. Spinas et tribulos germinabit tibi, et comedes herbam terrae [n: (Gen. III, 17)]. » Hic vero ager dictus est, postquam vomere et cultro terrae agressus faciem hanc horribilem deposuit, culturae respondit, cultoresque suos bonis fructibus exhilaravit. Ager vero dictus est ex hoc, quod agi coepit vomere, cultroque dejici, et (ut cultoribus mos est) sic in eodem loco subverti, ut apta sit suscipiendo semini, et eidem propagando, foecundari. Ad hunc igitur invitat agrum Sponsa suum Sponsum, dicens, « Veni, » id est, ut accessum habeam ad te, hoc consenti. « Egrediamur, » Tu de indicibili tuae majestatis abscondito assumpta carne egredere, id est, manifeste appare; egoque tecum de occultis meis, de immunditiis meis, de infidelitate [1295B] penitus egressa, te corde credens, te confitens, te humiliter adorans, tibi inseparabiliter adhaerens, tecum in agrum hunc venire parata sum, ut attendamus, an bene cultus sit, an huic verbi semina commendanda, et sit de eo spes ulla boni praestolanda. Sequitur:

*Commoremur in villis.*

Fiunt quidem habitationes in agris, ut dictum est de campo Sennaar, in quo civitas Babylon a filiis Noe constructa est [n: (Gen. XI, 2)]; fiunt oppida; fiunt et villae: in civitate divites, in oppidis potentes habitant; in villis vero minorum et humiliorum mansio est, quae tanto Deo gratior est, quanto humilior est, tanto magis acceptabilis est, quanto virtutis et doctrinae perceptibilis est. Hic Sponso moram facere, [1295C] et se Sponso commorari exoptat, ubi sancti sui corporis et sanguinis est consecratio, ubi peccatorum in baptismate fit ablutio, ubi delictorum quotidiana confessio, et fidelium populorum crebra Domino fit oblatio: hinc decimarum, hinc aliorum quoque munerum frequens largitio, et in exitu suo sacra Domini recognitio, et ipsorum ad aeternam beatitudinem transmigratio. Sequitur:

11. *Mane surgamus ad vineas: videamus si floruit vinea, si flores fructus parturiunt.*



## CAPUT VII. (cont.)

Ille beatus est, cujus a Domino vinea mane visitatur. Nam vinea cujusque praesens haec vita est; et mane unicuique est vitae praesentis inchoatio. Sunt vero quidam quos mane, id est, ab ipso vitae [1295D] exordio, visitat Deus, dirigit, et magnificat, et quod ex eis magni futuri sint fructus miraculorum, etiam exhibitione demonstrat; « Videamus si floruit vinea. » Ad hos Dilectum invitat Sponsa, ut cum his maneat, et hos florere faciat, et flores fructus parturientes ipse custodiat. Hi quidem nostri sunt in Deo profectus: nam ut vinea primo folia, deinde florem, inde fructum producit; sic in his quae Dei sunt, qui hunc videre et habere solliciti sunt, initiatio quaedam est a malo aversio; magnus enim profectus est, ad ea quae Dei sunt felix conversio. Summum vero in his est eorum quae Dei sunt, Deo placita dilectio, et in his opere beata completio. Unde et subditur:

*Si floruerint mala punica.*

[1296A]In malis quidem punicis amor indicatur martyrii. Majorem quidem dilectionem nemo habet, quam ut animam suam ponat quis pro amicis suis. Hunc quidem, cum omnes suos videre moneat, hos tamen praecipue, qui martyrii flagrant amore, qui vitam suam pro Christo ponere, et per mortem sursum ascendere desiderant, speciali quadam visitatione monet attendere. Unde et ait:

*Ibi dabo tibi ubera mea.*

Quae sunt haec ubera quae Sponso datura est Sponsa cum sic venerit, et Ecclesiam sic visitaverit? Ubera quidem ea pars corporis sunt, qua filios suos alit Ecclesia, qua ipsorum infantiam protrahit, et ipsos in robur juvenile producit; et cum in hoc robur excreverint, sibi, martyrioque quod desiderant, [1296B] ipsique ob quem desiderant, derelinquit. Ait igitur, « Ibi dabo tibi ubera mea, » id est, omnes mentis meae sinus aperiam, ut a te intelligam, quid cuique ordini dicendum sit, qualiter ordo quisque monendus, ut ad te veniat teque in aeternum possideat. Sequitur:

*Mandragorae dederunt odorem. In portis nostris omnia poma: nova et vetera, Dilecte mi, servavi tibi.*

Vocato Dilecto suo ut ad Ecclesiam veniat, ut illam visitet, et quae eum videre desiderat, istud adnectit, dicens, Ad hoc quidem quod expeto, difficilem te invenire non ambigo, quia mandragoras in portis nostris odorem tui jam dedisse intelligo. Mandragoras quidem Prophetas nominat, quae humani corporis formam retinent, et membrum quodque [1296C] corporis humani quod morbus occupat de membro simili, raso sibi pulvere curat. Haec quoque sterilem foecundam efficit, et multa medicinae prodest arte laborantibus: unde haec Prophetas exprimit, qui humanitatem Christi, et ea quae in homine gessit, exprimunt; et hoc in portis nostris, id est, Scripturis quae nostrae jam effectae sunt, exclamare et prophetare non desinunt. Haec quidem omnia poma, quae prophetae novi recentesque praedixerunt; « et vetera, » antiqua, scilicet, quae ab Adam usque nunc dicta sunt, tibi reservavi, quia sunt in te complenda, et ipso operis effectu demonstranda. Sequitur:



## CAPUT VIII.

1. *Quis mihi det te fratrem meum sugentem ubera [1296D] matris meae, ut inveniam te foris, et deosculer te, et jam me nemo despiciat. 2. Apprehendam te, et ducam in domum matris meae: ibi me docebis, et dabo tibi poculum ex vino condito, et mustum malorum granatorum meorum.*

Haec Sponsa de adventu Sponsi sui sollicita, jamdiu orans exoptavit, dicens, « Veni, Dilecte mi; Egrediamur in agrum; » et quod oravit, certo affuturum praedixit, quia hoc mandragorae praelocuti sunt, hoc omnes prophetae praedixerunt. Ergo de hoc quod certo futurum est, jam quaerit, dicens: « Quis mihi det te fratrem meum, » id est, tam dignus erit ut te fratrem meum mihi visibiliter ostendat, te in corporali forma mihi fratrem meum [1297A] demonstret. Antiquum enim est, et auditu cognitum, Deum Patrem omnium me inter caetera creasse, et mihi patrem inter caetera exstitisse, et me inter creaturas, ipsum semper quasi Patrem invocasse: sed quod ipse mihi frater sit, novum est et inauditum a seculis, et tamen mundo propagandum. Missus est enim Gabriel angelus ad Mariam, dicens, « Ave, gratia plena; Dominus tecum. Spiritus Sanctus superveniet in te, et virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Ideoque quod nascetur ex te sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei [n: (Luc. I, 28, 35)]. » Ecce quod Dei Filius, ex Virgine sancta natus, baptismo sancto regenitus, verae Ecclesiae filius effectus est, et nobis omnibus frater esse incepit, qui nobis ante omnia Pater exstitit. Unde post resurrectionem, [1297B] ait, « Ite, nunciate fratribus meis, ut eant in Galilaeam; ibi me videbunt [n: (Matth. XXVIII, 10)]. » Unde, ut quem Deum Patrem hucusque dixeram, jam fratrem mihi nomino; ideoque fratrem, quia sugentem ubera matris meae, Mariae, scilicet; quae ex hoc quod mater ejus effecta est, omnium digne mater est qui ipsum invocant, et ejus sibi opem in quacunque necessitate implorant. Per hanc quidem Dei Filius foris inventus est, id est, in hac forma corporali, quam de novo assumpsit, et in ipsa mundo apparuit, et in hac ab eo (ut dictum est) osculum sibi reconciliationis assumpsit; unde ait, « Et jam me nemo despiciat. » Antequam enim reconciliationis osculum Deus homini [1297C] porrexisset, homo et angelis, et daemonibus, sibi etiam ipsi despectibilis habebatur, qui totus in Infernum possidendus trahebatur. At postquam morte unigeniti reconciliatus est, Infernum deserens, regionem Paradisi possidere coepit et coeli, et extunc nec coeli possessoribus despectui habitus est, nec Inferni. Ait enim ipsa, « Apprehendam te, » id est, firmissimo amplexu tenebo te: non minis, non verberibus, non omni mortis genere amovebor aut avellar a te: et sic inducam te « in domum matris meae, » coelestis, scilicet, Jerusalem, quae erudit me, et exemplum mihi dilectionis ostendit, qua semper adhaeream tibi, et amoveri nequeam a te; et inducam te in « cubiculum genitricis meae, » id est, antiquum illud amoris habitaculum, quo te semper [1297D] tenuit genitrix mea, id est, antiquissima de patriarchis et prophetis, aliisque fidelibus exorta collectio, et, quae nunquam a te avelli potuit, sacra congregatio. « Ibi tu docebis me, » quia tunc erimus omnes docibiles Dei. Et nos quid tibi dabimus? « Poculum ex vino condito, » amorem, scilicet, sempiternum; qui tot modis formatus est, quod modis vina formari solent ex diversis speciebus; « Et mustum malorum granatorum meorum, » id est, passionem martyrum meorum, qui sibi sic in amoris dulcedine juncti sunt, ut sibi mala junguntur in malis, et nullis a te potuerunt malis averti. Sequitur:

3. *Laeva ejus sub capite meo; et dextera illius amplexabitur me. 4. Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem, ne suscitetis, [1298A] neque evigilare faciatis Dilectam, donec ipsa velit.*

Haec quia jam dicta sunt, non repetimus, sed ubi dicta sunt, studiosis legenda committimus. Sequitur:

5. *Quae est ista, quae ascendit de deserto, deliciis affluens, innixa super Dilectum suum?*

Amans amantem se facile respicit, et quae format amor, facile sibi verba transfundit. Unde quia ex jam dictis diligentis se Sponsae facile denotatur affectus, Sponsus ei subito responsum praestat amoris, quaerens et sciscitans, quae illa est: non quod ignoret eam, sed ut neminem ignorare permittat. Qualis sit, et quanta, quantaque admiratione dignissima, quae sic de deserto ascendit? Mundum [1298B] hunc desertum nominans, quem plures ut patriam inhabitare conantur, et suo fraudati conamine, hinc ad inferna descendunt, et sic, quae sit eis patria destinata, cognoscunt. Hoc desertum est locus iste, quem Dominus ascendendo deseruit, cum multis videntibus in coelum elevatus ascendit. Quare sequitur, haec ipsa « potens in deliciis, » quibus affluens, quasque Domino summe placere intelligens, ei fide recta, spe robusta, charitate fervida quaerit assistere, et haec sibi ab ipso data praesentare. Hoc vero est quod ait, Quae, quantique meriti haec est, quae deserto hoc mundo, scilicet, quem Deus hinc ascendendo deseruit, qui aliis descensionis locus esse consuevit, locum sibi faciens ascensionis, in alta prosilit, virtutum delicias praesentans [1298C] Deo, quas sibi ab ipso collatas esse cognoscit? Altius vero beatus Gregorius, aspiciens super haec, ait, Ecclesia verborum Dei deliciis affluens, de praesenti deserto ad superiora ascendit. Deliciis affluere est, in amore Dei epulis Scripturarum satiari. Deliciis ergo affluens ascendit, quia nos mysticis intelligentiis pastos, ad superna quotidie sublevat, in cujus verbis tot sunt deliciae, quot sunt diversitates spiritualis intelligentiae. Modo nos pascit historia, reficit moralis allegoria, aliquando suspendit contemplatio ad altiora. Anima his deliciis affluens, mystico intellectu reficitur, in quo praesens obscuritas fulgore diei subsequentis illuminatur, ut etiam in hac corruptione in intellectum illius [1298D] veri luminis erumpat, et verborum deliciis pasta, praegustando discat, quid de pabulo veritatis esuriat. Sequitur:

*Sub arbore malo suscitavi te: ibi corrupta est mater tua: ibi violata est genitrix tua.*

Dictum est, quod ista deliciis affluens, super Dilectum suum innixa est: jam, quod illi inniti potuerit et debuerit, consequenter demonstratur. Ait enim, « Sub arbore malo suscitavi te, » id est, a morte revocavi te; sub arbore malo quidem constitutam, id est, peccato obnoxiam, quod arbore malo contractum est. Dicunt enim vetitam illam arborem, a qua homo in Paradiso abstinere jussus est, malum fuisse, et lignum illud quod bonum esset ad vescendum, et pulchrum oculis, aspectuque delectabile, [1299A] in concupiscentiam mulieri devenisse; quae de illo tulit, viroque porrexit, seque ream inobedientiae, posterosque, constituit. Ab hoc quidem inobedientiae malo Sponsus iste crucem sustinens, omnes eripuit, ideoque seipsam sub malo, id est, sub peccato quod ex malo contractum est, positam suscitasse et redemisse confitetur. Quod ne modicum aestimetur, adjungit, « Ibi corrupta est mater tua; ibi violata est genitrix tua; » matrem vocans generationem omnem, quae ab Adam ad Abraham usque protracta est: genitricem vero illam nominans, quae ab Abraham usque ad Christum, arctiori quadam mandatorum lege constricta est, per hos edocens omnes humana generatione procreatos, delicto huic obnoxios; nisi eos aut Spiritus, antequam [1299B] nascerentur, sanctificaret, utpote sanctam Virginem quae Dei constituta est habitaculum, Joannem Baptistam, et Jeremiam, quos sanctificatos ab utero cognoscimus, aut eis suo Deus sacramento subveniret. Quod si quis altius curat inspicere, tractatum relegat, quem supra de reconciliationis osculo disseruimus, et quae nobis, dictante Domino, donata sunt, exposuimus. Sequitur.

6. *Pone me ut signaculum super cor tuum, ut signaculum super brachium tuum.*

Quia liberavi te a morte quam meruisti, per mortem crucis meae; ideo tibi consequenter injungo, ut me, id est, meam dilectionem, qua homo [1299C] pro te factus sum, qua pro te crucifixus sum, qua humiliavi me, ut de morte quam merueras eruerem te, ponas semper ut signaculum, id est, ut memoriale quoddam, super cor tuum, id est, in corde tuo; ut in omni eo quod agere disposueris, hanc semper attendas dilectionem, ne quid effectu complere praesumas, nisi id huic dilectioni cohaerere conspicias. Idem et de brachio subjungit, « Ut signaculum super brachium tuum. » Haec enim si cohaerentia sunt, cor deliberans, et brachium id quod corde deliberatur exsequens. Quae si ambo memoriale hujus dilectionis teneant, ab omni se opere, quod huic non convenit dilectioni, cohibebunt. Sic cor muniens et brachia, hoc quod alias dictum est, persuadet: alias namque dictum est, « Sex sunt quae [1299D] odit Dominus, et septimum detestatur anima ejus: Oculos sublimes, linguam mendacem, manus effundentes innoxium sanguinem, cor machinans cogitationes pessimas, pedes veloces ad currendum in malum, proferentem mendacia testem fallacem, et eum qui seminat inter fratres discordias [n: (Prov. VI, 16, 17, 18, 19)]. » Quae quidem omnia, si dilectionem Dei habeas, si hanc in corde tuo et in brachio, ut memoriale defigas, longe fient a te, nec est quod in modico impediant te.

*Quia fortis est ut mors dilectio*

Mors quidem fortis est, quia reges exterminat, tyrannos dejicit, divites spoliat, omne denique [1300A] quod in mundo vivit rapit ad se, uno communi fine cuncta terminans, et universa concludens: sic et Christi vera dilectio fortis quidem est, Christo quaeque adversantia respuens, non exhorrens gladium, non timens carcerem, vincula non metuens, omne quod excogitari potest supplicii [cn: 71 | F. suppl. *genus*] libens in se suscipiens, haec non tormenta reputans, sed ut suae salutis adjumenta venerans et adorans. Excogitavit mundus bestias, excogitavit ardentes laminas, rotas excogitavit et cochleas; quae tamen omnia superavit et vicit charitas manens in horum cordibus, quos expugnabat malignitas. Unde non ut mors fortis, sed ipsa morte fortior est ista dilectio, quae in eam irruente morte manet integra, et per eam praemia consequi meretur aeterna. Sequitur:

[1300B] *Et dura sicut infernus aemulatio.*

Ut dilectio commendatur, sic improbatur aemulatio; aemulatio enim dicitur invida charitatis imitatio. Quidam enim videntes martyres honorari, et sanctos ab omnibus confessores venerari, invidentes iis honoribus, et eosdem cupientes, se quasi sequaces martyrum et ipsorum imitatores praeferebant, et sic se martyres, aut quasi martyres aestimabant: quorum studia Sponsus ipse sic improbat, dicens, « Dura sicut infernus aemulatio. » Nam sicut Infernus, quos rapit hos trahit, nec eorum quemquam extrahi a se permittit; sic istorum dura est conditio, quae sic coadunatur inferno, bonum sibi tantum simulans dolo malo. Sequitur:



## CAPUT VIII. (cont.)

[1300C] *Lampades ejus lampades ignis atque flammarum. 7. Aquae multae non potuerunt exstinguere charitatem, nec flumina obruent illam.*

Haec charitatis commendatio est, quae est vera Dei dilectio; ejus enim lampades ignis, sunt corda scilicet, sanctorum, in modum formata lampadum, quae hinc stricta, superius vero dilatata sunt, et in spiritualis ignis habitaculum praeparata. Qui quidem ignis, semper ignis est, semper calefaciens, et in dilectione Dei cor semper accendens; aliquando ignis cum flamma, quando non solum ardet et accendit, immo lucet in opere, et quod intus agit, manifestat in re; ita quidem, quod aquae multae non possunt hanc charitatem extinguere: hanc enim dilectionem tribulationes nullae, nullae vexationum [1300D] adinventiones possunt extinguere; quia quo mala multiplicantur, in Deum hinc constat ipsum excrescere, quia « flumina non obruent illum, » id est, mala malis aggregata in nullo Dei gratiae praevalebunt. Sequitur:

*Si dederit homo omnem substantiam domus suae pro dilectione, quasi nihil despiciet eam.*

Haec consummata laus ejus est: nam si totum quod temporaliter acquiritur homo dederit, ut hanc sibi charitatem acquirat, eam totam substantiam quasi nil despiciet, et nil sibi dedisse videbitur, quia charum et amabile est quod acquiritur. Sequitur:

[1301A]

## 8.

*Soror nostra parva, et ubera non habet. Quid faciemus sorori nostrae in die quando alloquenda est.*

A Sponso Sponsa commendata est, et quod ab eo de morte redempta sit, commonuit, et quod hoc memoriale cordis habeat, edocta; edocta quoque quod charitas vincat omnia; ipsa quidem omnia grata habet et suscipit; et jam de charitate commonita, quaestionem annectit, dicens, « Soror nostra parva, et ubera non habet. » Venit sibi in mentem, quod ait Apostolus, « Cum plenitudo Gentium intraverit, tunc omnis Israel salvus fiet [n: (Rom. XI, 25, 26)]. Hujus itaque synagogae reminiscitur, quae ad praesens in tenebris ambulat, Christum negat, quae de illo dicuntur et creduntur, haec blasphemat. [1301B] Hanc itaque sanctum apostolum in novissimis convertendam, et Eliam, et Henoch ad hos convertendos a Christo reservatos praesciens, hanc propter conversionem futuram sororem nominans, ex charitate sic ait, « Soror nostra parva, et ubera non habet: » parva quidem fide, spe minima, in charitate jam nulla. Haec ubera non habet, nulla in se doctrinae retinacula continet; quae propter se facta sunt, haec negat et reticet. Hanc ergo ad fidem in novissimo venturam praesciens, a Sponso sic quaerit, « Quid faciemus sorori nostrae, in die quando alloquenda est? » Quid dicemus? Illam quomodo commonebimus? Quae illi verba salutis dabimus? Ad haec interrogata sic respondet Sponsus:

*[1301C]*

## 9.

*Si murus est, aedificemus super eum propugnacula argentea: si ostium est, compingamus illud tabulis cedrinis.*

Eorum enim qui convertendi sunt, quidam sunt ut murus, magnam habentes in se scientiam, literarum quoque notitiam, et ob hoc quoque muri, contra se impugnantes, duritiam; quibus ait Sponsus, ut aedificentur super eos propugnacula argentea, id est, divinarum scripturarum eis dentur testimonia, et autoritatum quibus praemunimur; his donentur insignia, quibus hi jam muniti Ecclesiae verae sunt defensores et tutela. « Si vero ostium est, compingamus illud tabulis cedrinis. » Ostium vero sunt hi, per quos quidam intrant, quidam vero exeunt: qui quidem minores sunt scientia, [1301D] minus quidem eruditi scripturis, quibus non summa proponenda sunt, et intellectu difficilia, sed tabulae compingendae sunt cedrinae, id est, leves Scripturae proponendae; ut est ea tabula quam pinxit Dominus, dicens, « Beati pauperes spiritu: quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum. Beati mites: quoniam ipsi possidebunt terram. Beati qui lugent: quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Beati, qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam; quoniam ipsi saturabuntur [n: (Matth. V, 3 et seq.)]. » Quae quidem tabula cedrina est, imputribilis, scilicet, et sententias proferens incontaminatas, veras et infringibiles. Aliaeque tabulae his similes, quae his propositae, ipsos in veritate suscepta adjuvare poterunt et confirmare. Sequitur

*[1302A]*



## 10.

*Ego murus: et ubera mea sicut turris; ex quo facta sum coram eo quasi pacem reperiens.*

Audito Dilecti responso, quo Sponsam monet, ut et conversae synagogae propugnacula proponat argentea, et ad defensionem Ecclesiae propugnatores mittat idoneos, ipsa congratulanter ait, « Ego murus, » me quoque ipsam opponam ictibus; et ubera mea, praelati, scilicet, Ecclesiarum, quos mea ob hoc ubera nomino, quod meo eos lacte nutrio, hi mecum erunt Ecclesiae firma et inexpugnabilis defensio, et mecum aeternae vitae incontradicibilis acquisitio; eo quod reddita jam mihi sorore mea quae perierat, « Facta sum coram eo quasi pacem reperiens. » Tunc enim vere pax reperta erit, cum nullus eorum qui praesciti sunt ad vitam jam deerit, [1302B] sed omnes suos Ecclesia intra se jam continens, summa prosperitate gaudebit. Sequitur:

11. *Vinea fuit pacifico in ea, quae habet populos: tradidit eam custodibus.*

Consummata jam laude cantici hujus, et consummata plenitudine Sponsae hujus, cum sibi synagoga, quam sororem nominat, ad fidem conversa erit, et ad fidem Gentium plenitudo intraverit, de se tota jam Sponsa loquitur, dicens, « Vinea fuit pacifico. » Ego quidem cum plenitudine Gentium jam vocata, cum synagoga jam ad fidem conversa, exstiti vinea pacifico, id est, Jesu Christo Domino nostro, qui pacificavit omnia quae in terra sunt, et quae in coelo. « In ea quae habet populos, » id est, in multitudine Gentium, quae tota a Deo creata est, sed [1302C] non tota ad vitam praeordinata; « Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci vero electi [n: (Matth. XX, 16)]. » Ego vero cum omnium electorum, Judaeorum et Gentium multitudine, vinea fui pacifico, electos sibi fructus faciens, dignos ab eo suscipi, dignos Deo Patri praesentari. Quam quidem vineam dicit pacificum tradidisse custodibus: nam pars Ecclesiae quae ab Adam usque ad Christum exstitit, Patriarchis, et Prophetis, et Legis sanctae Doctoribus custodienda commissa est. Quae vero a Christo usque in finem seculi futura est, apostolis sanctis, et martyribus, aliisque honore pollentibus erudienda, concessa est. Sequitur:

[1302D] *Vir affert pro fructu ejus mille argenteos. 12. Vinea mea coram me est. Mille tui pacifici, et ducenti his qui custodiunt fructus ejus.*

Hanc quidem vineam pacificus excoluit, plantavit, et secuit, et ad florem, fructumque perduxit; quae non in amaritudinem conversa est, nec labruscas fecit, sed elegantes uvas, et Deo Patri praesentari dignissimas. Unde hic dicitur, « Vir affert pro fructu ejus mille argenteos. » Quis iste vir est? Vir ille bonus, cujus meminit David, dicens, « Vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, et in via peccatorum non stetit, et in cathedra pestilentiae non sedit. Sed in lege Domini voluntas ejus, et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte [n: (Psal. I, 1, 2)]. » Hic solus, vir dici dignissimus, fructus suscipit Ecclesiae, [1303A] offertque Deo Patri, a quo, ad remunerandam Ecclesiam, mille suscipit argenteos, quos affert, ut ditetur Ecclesia, et se bene fructificasse congaudeat. Per mille vero argenteos vitam denotat aeternam, ejusque beatitudinem infinitam, qua suos remunerabit Dominus, cum eos praesentaverit Patri, et his in coelestibus sedes collocaverit. Hanc vero beatitudinem numero millenario comprehendi designat, quae quarta unitas est: prima enim unitas, unitas ipsa est; secunda, denarius; tertia, centenarius; quarta, millenarius; post hunc in infinitum numerus extenditur, habens millenarium sibi semper radicem et unitatem. Bene ergo per hunc, infinitas; et per argentum, beatitudinis excellentia demonstratur; de hac enim dictum est, « Eloquia [1303B] Domini, eloquia casta: argentum igne examinatum, probatum terrae, purgatum septuplum [n: (Psal. XI, 7)]. » Quia quae Dominum praedicant eloquia, castitatem in se continentia sunt, nullam in se haeresin, nullam prorsus incontinentiam admittentia, sed sunt in se velut argentum igne sancti Spiritus examinatum, quo nihil dulcius tinnit eloquio, nihil animae plus sapidum; quo nil a terra probatius, quo nil igne septiformis spiritus purgatius invenitur: de qua responsum hoc Patris accipit, « Vinea mea coram me est, » id est, Omnis haec electorum multitudo mihi complacet, in omni cogitatu et opere mecum est, quam tu mihi per pacificos mille significas, et per ducentos, qui custodiunt fructus ejus. Hi namque perfecti illi sunt, qui ab Adam usque ad [1303C] Christum universitatem hanc verbis erudierunt, exemplis custodierunt, et meritis ornaverunt. Centum vero qui supersunt, sunt ii qui a Christo usque in finem seculi electae illi multitudini praefuerunt: hi Deo Patri praesentantur, et in aeterna beatitudine, cum his quibus praefuerant coronantur. Sequitur:

13. *Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant: fac me audire vocem tuam.*

Haec Sponsi est ultima commonitio, qua Sponsam de laude sua commonet, dicens, « Quae habitas in hortis, fac me audire vocem tuam. » Haec quidem jam in hortis Judaea primatum obtinens, ipsam jam fide conversam retinens, hanc praeceptis vitae erudiens, [1303D] gentilitatis quoque multitudinem plene possidens, in hortis virtutum plane residens, virtutes omnes quae Domino suave redolent in se continens, bene in hortis Ecclesiarum habitare dicitur, et ut ab ea laus Domino proferatur, monitis coelestibus exposcitur, cum dicitur Quae habitas in hortis Ecclesiarum, [1304A] fac me audire vocem tuam, ut a cunctis Ecclesiis laus mea resonet, et ab omni laus mea cum gratiarum actione resultet. « Amici » enim « auscultant; » Angeli namque, et omnes cum his virtutes angelicae, Christo cum his fidelis amicitiae ab initio virtute conjunctae, exspectant et auscultant gloriam remunerationis meae, quam jam sperant in gloria laudis tuae. Sequitur:

14. *Fuge Dilecte mi, et assimilare capreae hinnuloque cervorum super montes aromatum.*

Haec est Ecclesiae ultima responsio, qua respondet Sponsa Dilecto suo, dicens, « Fuge, Dilecte mi. » Hanc Sponsus de laude commonet, hortatur ut laudem personet, non quod velit, quod nunc cantica laudis incipiat, sed exspectata communi omnium resurrectione, [1304B] cum Sponsus in nube venerit, cum ejus adventum angelus clara voce personuerit, dicens, « Ecce Sponsus venit, Exite obviam ei [n: (Matth. XXV, 6)]; » cum ad [cn: 72 | F. *resuscitandum*.] resurgendum omnes tuba lugubris insonuerit, et Judex stipatus Angelis, in sede suae majestatis sederit, et ei, nullo excepto, mundus occurrerit, et horrendam in reprobos sententiam tulerit, et dederit electis suis omnibus sententiam quam dicturus est, « Venite, benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum a constitutione mundi. » Tunc quidem Ecclesiae cum sanctis omnibus personabit laus et gratiarum actio, qualis audita non est a seculo, cunctique ejus laudis participes in secula benedicentur a Domino. Quod quia diligenti se Sponsae praemonstratum est, ideo non [1304C] indignando, sed moram hanc patienter sustinendo, sic respondet, « Fuge, Dilecte mi, » quod est, a nostris te conspectibus ad praesens abstrahe; in hoc similis assistens capreae hinnuloque cervorum, quae munda quidem animalia sunt, et a conspectibus hominum se in jugis montium continentia. Quos quidem montes, ubi iste cervorum hinnulus habitat, ut a caeteris montibus discernat, addit, « aromatum. » Montes enim aromatum sunt sancta angelorum agmina, virtutumque omnium coelestium habitacula, a quibus spirant omnes aromatizantes gratiae, quas certum est Domino complacere. His Dominus de se vitae diffundit balsamum, ut eo peruncti jam vivant in aeternum: cui nimirum unctioni, Ecclesia se participem [1304D] fieri desiderans, et ad hanc semper in his quae dicta sunt suspirans, osculum sibi dari sanctissimae jucunditatis expetiit, et jam nunc quod illud sit acceptura post paululum cum tota sui plenitudine, certissima Sponsi sui promissione certificata conquiescit.
english:
## DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

*To the most reverend and most ample prelate, the lord WILLIAM JUXON, bishop of London and Lord High Treasurer of England, PATRICK YOUNG. Greeting.*

That oblivion has full often, *most Ample and [sic: Reverendissim] Prelate,* given occasion for a more renowned fame, and that many things have fallen in order that they might afterwards rise again more adorned, is a thing to which assurance is given and abundant witness borne not only by deserted ruined walls and by rubble long neglected, which, laid low by age, put on a new face and a more august form: but by the monuments of genius also, which are day by day corrected, are published in more emended form, and by the sedulous diligence of the studious are drawn forth, first out of mould and dust, into the light and into the day. Among these is this devout and elegant writing of thy predecessor, which until now has perhaps lain buried in oblivion, that in this learned age it might emerge from the darkness with a greater splendour, and might look again, under the auspices of thy most celebrated name, upon the light which it had first drunk in within thy walls. His aged infirmities, or rather those of the age in which he lived, which occur here and there in phrasing or in matter: if, out of your singular piety, *Your most Ample Lordship* be willing to cover them with but the hem of your own garment, and to deem him worthy of your patronage together with his *Acoluthus* (for to go forth into public alone, without a companion, was neither seemly, nor did the condition of so great a man allow it), and kindly to interpret this our small labour in publishing the two, you will make a step toward greater things, which may hereafter be dedicated to thy name, and will bind me, most devoted to *Thy Amplitude,* by a closer bond of observance for the time to come. Given the day before the Nones of November. In the year MDCXXXVIII.

## GILBERT'S PREFACE.

[1147A]To his lord and most dear friend Robert, by the grace of God bishop of Hereford, brother Gilbert, humble minister of the Church of London: to be exercised in those things which are God's, and in the same to be consummated with a most blessed end.

Lest the authority of thy command, my lord, should seem to me empty or cheap, I have straightway sent thee the book which thou didst ask for: the book, that is, which with the Lord's help I lately put forth upon the Song of Songs, and which I entrusted to no man before thee, either to be copied or to be looked into. For it was not written by me for praise, nor for the sake of a public commendation, but that I might hold in memory the things which, the Lord teaching, I had learned: and that I might show that these things are not, after the manner of the Jews, to be cheaply despised, but to be read humbly with the inmost understanding, and to be understood in the same spirit in which they [1148A] were spoken. And when it had been read through by thee with the utmost attention from beginning to end, thou didst receive it with much alacrity of mind, and, as I hear, didst commend with much praise that I had applied my zeal to this study: and, that nothing might be wanting to its perfection, thou didst ask that a Prologue be fitted to it by me, so that the completion of the work might be worthy, and to it a rendering of thanks be made; for it is written, « Love is strong as death [n: (Cap. VIII, 6)]. » For as there is nothing mortal that can break the bond of death, so there is nothing possible that the urgency of love cannot obtain. This it was that emptied the Lord, and bound him with human bonds; this it was that, after the cross and the sepulchre, led him down to the lowest seats, that he might snatch thence those who had believed that he would come, [1149A] and were diligently awaiting him: this it is that reforms into the liberty of grace those whom, at the dictate of justice, it had made sons of wrath, mercy tempering judgment. This changes my purpose, so that I set a prologue to a work which I undertook to expound without a prologue. For the author of the work was Solomon, who imitated the ancient writers, who do not make their readers attentive by prefixing a prologue, but by showing them the matter of which they are about to treat arouse their attention, and turn their zeal toward the recognition of the things that are said. Whence that saying of Moses: « In the beginning God created heaven and earth: but the earth was without form, » [var: Vulg. *inanis et vacua*, "void and empty"] etc. [n: (Gen. I, 1)]. And that of Exodus: « These are the names of the sons of Israel, who entered into Egypt with Jacob [n: (Exod. I, 1)]. » So, [1149B] running through the whole Pentateuch, thou wilt find the books of Judges and of Kings, and the others besides, written without a prologue; and if prologues have been added to them, thou wilt recognize that they were added long afterwards, after the coming of the Saviour. Imitating these, Solomon begins straightway from the very matter of which he is about to treat, knowing that the matter itself which is handled has in itself either a manifest usefulness, by which it may allure, or an evident reason, by which one may despise the things coveted, or theological considerations, by which one may cast these [1150A] from the mind, and cleave to him alone who is the founder and creator of them. Three books therefore he made, which he does not adorn or enlarge with prologues: one, of « Parables »; another, « Ecclesiastes »; this third, « Sirasirim ». In the « Parables » he allures men to the possessing of those things by which the present life is furnished, that a man's own necessity may be relieved, that in the things wherein there is need his neighbour may be succoured, and that to the indigent there be given as necessity requires. But in « Ecclesiastes » he warns that the mind be not entangled [sic: implieetur] in these things, that love be not bent toward the things which are transitory: but that it judge them as vain, and decide upon and desire the things that are higher than these. Whence, adding « Sirasirim » next in order (which is called the « Song of songs »), in which, flying past all things, the soul stands beside the divine majesty, [1150B] embracing him as a bridegroom, and presenting to him out of her affection all that love can be. The soul, therefore, or the Church, kindled with the fire of love, not seeking these visible things but sighing after the invisible with the whole affection of the heart and the whole intention of the mind, he thus brings in: as one seeking God, yet not yet apprehending him, and, that she may hold him as apprehended, saying these things.

## EXPOSITION ON THE SONG OF SONGS.



## CHAPTER ONE.

[1149C]

1. *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.*

Who is this, so renowned? of form and grace so elegant? that, boldly seeking the kiss of the highest King, she says, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth? » Is this soul acting in a dream, feigning for herself what she wills, snatching herself away into some hope without substance, forming empty visions within herself, and even now hoping to apprehend what she could not obtain by laborious endeavours? For whither has this spirit ascended, so unmindful of gold and so forgetful of silver, accounting the precious stone as nothing, so spurning all that the world possesses and imparts to its own to be possessed, that, thrusting these away with the hand of holy perfection, she says: Stand apart, you; my love, withdrawn from you, [1149D] has been carried over into the things above, seeking him alone who alone truly is, and who furnishes to all things alike the cause and the effect of their being; sighing after whom, and impatient of holy desire, this soul communes with herself, and speaks, saying, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth: » for a soul so inspired speaks not vain things, but the highest. Long since has she drunk up the streams of Solomon's wisdom, and heard him disputing in « Ecclesiastes »: for once indeed, dainty and tender, when she had not yet come from outward forms to inward things, when she had not yet ascended from the creature to the Creator, [1150C] she clung to the world with all her embraces, and bound herself with all her affections to the very things that are seen: but having entered the school of spiritual doctrine, she was accounted worthy to hear no common master, but that Solomon supreme in wisdom, appointing for holy Church a certain introductory lesson, by which he might call away every elect soul from the world, and might join her, once called away and drawn apart, to him who is above the world, by the indissoluble bond of charity. For that supreme Solomon, seeing in the spirit that almost every soul was as it were digging in the earth, entangling herself in secular business, and no longer lifting her love upward but bending it lower; in order that he might raise up the bowed and wretched one, came down from the height of his own contemplation to the depths of human converse, calling back [1150D] the wanderer, instructing and reforming her with saving precepts, and so at length, by certain steps as it were of ascent, leading her through to the heights of holy contemplation and of love. First of all, therefore, he promises great things to the tender age, saying, « The parables of Solomon: to know wisdom and discipline, and to understand the words of prudence, and to receive the instruction of doctrine [n: (Prov. I, 1 seq.)]. » He suggests winning things, adding, « A wise man hearing shall be wiser, and he that understandeth shall possess governments. » Thus he does not at once preach to her contempt of the world and of the things that are in the world, [1151A] nor rehearse the hard and lofty matters of a straiter life; « for first that which is animal, then that which is spiritual [n: (I Cor. XV, 46)]. » Whence the best of masters, lest by urging weighty things at once he should blunt at the very beginnings the soul which he had taken up to be instructed, permits her, as though for the passing of her years of infancy, to use freely the world and the things that are of the world, and to take delight in them: yet appointing her a law, that she flow not away in sinning, nor turn to the use of malice and of lust what she has received by the great gift of a great author. He sets forth, therefore, to her who now listens attentively, the Parables; and with as many Parables as he instructs her, with so many laws does he inform and bind her to living well and honourably: which Parables indeed, if a prudent reader shall look into them more attentively with the eye of the mind, [1151B] he will understand that within them there is assigned most fully, for an honourable converse, a form of life for the possessors of this world and for those who pass their days in the common life. For because « without faith it is impossible to please God [n: (Heb. XI, 6)], » in the very opening of the treatise faith and the worship of the highest Godhead are inculcated, when it is said, « Hear, my son, the discipline of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother [n: (Prov. I, 8)]. » For the discipline of the highest Father, which the Church has most fully learned from him, is this: « To believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder to them that love him [n: (Heb. XI, 6)], » [var: Vulg. *inquirentibus se*, "to them that seek him"] and that in the end of the times he sent his Son in the flesh, and through him fulfilled his promises. But of the law of our mother the Church, the first is that natural law, engraved by the finger of God on the hearts of men; the second, that written upon tablets [1151C] of stone; the third, the law of the Gospel, ministered in the Holy Spirit and in grace. To forsake not the law of our mother, therefore, is this: not to withdraw from the unity of the Church, and from the worship of the highest Godhead, which she received inwardly by the inspiration of grace. But the remaining commandments of the Decalogue shine forth in distinct places throughout the whole volume of the Parables; and by these, and by very many other precepts besides, there is set forth as it were a certain secular holiness, and the life of secular men is ordered by a fit governance of reason; so that a man may so use the world as not to turn aside from God, and so possess the things permitted and made subject to him as unceasingly to abstain from the things forbidden. In the first instruction, since satisfaction has been made to human desires, and it has been permitted to man to use temporal things soberly, according to what was said to the first man [1151D] by the divine voice, « Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and rule over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and all things that move upon the earth [n: (Gen. I, 28)]; » there is now place for a second instruction, that concerning the things which man has long possessed he may now hear what judgment is to be made: whether he is to cleave to them with love, or whether love is to be raised from them to something higher and far better: whence Solomon, running through with the pen of truth each several thing that is under the sun, says in the second volume, « Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity [n: (Eccle. I, 2)]; » and mightily showing that this vanity is present in all transitory things, that the mind is by no means to be wrapped up in vain things, nor love to be entangled in vain things, [1152A] he sets apart from vanity the soul which he had taken up to be instructed, and applies her separately to truth, when at the end of that same work he adds, « Youth and pleasure are vain [n: (cap. XI, 10)]. » And a little after, « Remember thy Lord thy Creator in the days of thy youth, before the time of affliction come, and the years of which thou shalt say, they please me not [n: (Cap. XII, 1)]. » And a little after, in the very close of the discourse, « Fear God, and keep his commandments: this is every man [n: (ibid., 13)]. » By which compendious close of words, what else does he instil into the minds of men but the fear of that highest Godhead, and the reverence of the worship that is owed. For this is the way, this is the access to life, if the mind, seized with holy fear, always turn aside from unlawful things, and the mind, kindled within with the fire of love, [1152B] be unceasingly girded for good things: for man has been set midway in the order of the rational creature, having the good Angel above him, the evil one below, and, when this life has slipped away, he is to be brought to an equality with the one or the other according to the merits of his life. He therefore, as he is midway between these, so has something in common with each: love, namely, with him who is above, fear with him who is below: for the evil angels fear and tremble, but the good love perfectly; and as the evil angel does not rise up to love, so the good angels do not come down to fear, according to that saying, « Perfect charity casteth out fear [n: (I Joan. IV, 18)]. » Since, therefore, love alone wholly carries the good angel into itself, while fear alone presses the evil one downward, [1152C] there is not, apart from man, in the order of the whole creation, any in whom fear runs together with love, in whom these two meet joined to one another. To man, therefore, it is said, « Fear God, and keep his commandments: this is every man: » as if it were said, All this, that is, the whole of this, namely, « to fear, » and by loving « to keep the commandments, » belongs to man; that by fearing he may turn aside wrath, and by loving may attain to grace. Or if it be said, « This is every man, » that is, through fear and love a man is made perfect. Or, « This is every man, » that is, unto this every man is created, this does not differ from the same understanding, since this is the manner and the cause of his creation: that he should so escape wrath, and merit grace.



## CHAPTER ONE. (cont.)

This soul, therefore, receiving the admonitions of salvation not now drawn off [1152D] from afar, but from the fountain itself, that is, from the highest Solomon; taught already in the Proverbs in what manner she may possess worldly things, and in Ecclesiastes by what reasoning she may now forsake and despise in her mind the things she has possessed; hears now at last in the Songs how she may pass over from things visible to things invisible, and cleave to the author of all with the whole strength of her mind and the fullness of her affection. Thus, from the moral discipline by which she holily shares what she possesses, through the rational, by which she rightly judges of worldly things, having entered upon that holy and highest *theoria*, having now utterly forgotten the things that are behind, climbing that holy mountain and the summit of her own mind, she follows through the midst of the cloud and the darkness that holy Moses to the heights of contemplation; [1153A] where, abiding in a secret dwelling [n: (Exod. XIX, 20, et XX, 21)], she seeks not lofty panelled ceilings, nor the painted flanks of attendants, nor acres of fields stretched out beyond measure, but, that she may abound plentifully in all things, seeks him alone who is all things, who is the light and the rest of souls, the fount of good things and the origin of virtues, whom to apprehend is the highest thing, and whom to enjoy the most delightful: and being driven within by desire of him, she utters what she feels, and no longer restraining herself within the cloisters of silence, speaks, after the manner of a lover, either to herself or to some heavenly Virtue akin to her, saying, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. » Love indeed errs rather often in judgment, and while it is borne headlong by its own desire, whithersoever it has turned itself it seems to itself to behold the thing it desires, and that any other person too [1153B] experiences in himself what it feels: whence, as though it were plain to others who it is that love draws and as it were absorbs into itself, when she utters outwardly what she does within, she designates no one by name, but with a certain discreet indiscretion so says, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. » This indeed is the secret of a perfect mind, and the soliloquy of a soul now cleansed with the heavenly Bridegroom. Come then, turn aside the edge of thy mind a little, and for a short while come down from the highest things to the lower; consider a soul still bound fast by unbelief, one who has not yet been enlightened to receive the rays of faith, has not yet touched the thresholds of the Church, and knew nothing at all of the Bridegroom: wilt thou judge that the Song rightly belongs to her? that she should speak to the Bridegroom of holy souls, saying, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth? » Would not [1153C] this Parable be unseemly in her mouth? But if thou consider a soul enlightened indeed by faith, yet dead in works, grievously oppressed and overwhelmed by sins, making for herself a long rope of sin, and not running back to the good by that remedy of penance: can the Song rightly be fitted to her, that, misshapen of mouth, and of horrid face, and foul in all her body, she should nevertheless say to the Father of all, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. » But a soul fortified by faith and imbued with the sacraments, now raising herself by the law of the mind to the good of virtue, now, in the lapse into sin, taking upon her the law that fights back in her members; subject to this alternation, mourning, and in her mourning crying aloud: « O who shall deliver me from the body of this death? » [1153D] [n: (Rom. VII, 24.)] Will she fitly sing the Song, that, overcast with the tears of sadness and drawing the sobs of penance, she should say, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. »

But if, advancing a little, thou consider a soul upon a certain higher step, governing herself by a kind of even moderation, so that she neither now admits the sins for which damnation is due, nor yet climbs to the heights of virtue, dwelling in a manner with Lot in Segor, not yet reaching the mountains: she assuredly, in proportion as she does not yet touch the summits of virtue, is the more delighted by outward things, and burns less strongly in the desire of the heavenly kiss; so that neither to her does that rightly belong which was said, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his [1154A] mouth. » Enter now at last the secret place of the spiritual soul; consider a soul now established in grace, whom the spirit has drawn out into the mountains, who has now determined to dwell on the heights, who, the world being now overcome, has trodden sin underfoot, who, running after the Lord with Peter, has now said, « Behold, we have left all things, and have followed thee [n: (Matth. XIX, 27)]; » she, though she be far from the darkness of unbelief, from the reign of sin and of death, from the assault of temptation, from the torpor of the mind, does not yet presume so far as to dare, where she awaits the kiss of the highest King, which perhaps she has not yet tasted, saying, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth: » but either she sits content, with Mary, with the kiss of the holy feet, or, according to John, « she stands with the friends of the Bridegroom, and rejoiceth with joy at his voice [n: (Joan. III, 29)], » [1154B] which voice, most full of sweetness, she has now been accounted worthy to hear within, and in a certain appearance and promise of things to come alike to be delighted and to rest. From hence ascend, if now thou canst, to the sixth step of perfection, by which a love now consecrated enters the heights of contemplation; where the Lord is transfigured upon the mountain for her, and that most holy Moses, hidden from human eyes, now privy to the heavenly secrets, rests most sweetly in the very hidden place of the Godhead: here the most blessed soul, contemplating in her heart the King whom she loves, and stretched out toward God as far as in this life is lawful, is refreshed by the sweetness of the eternal vision; and, turning back the eye of contemplation upon all things that have been created, while she wonders not so much at them as at [1154C] the wisdom of the highest Maker in them, and at his unspeakable power, disdaining all that is created, gathers herself wholly into that wisdom, and is bound fast to it by the bond of charity and by the light of contemplation; and while she sees that all that is comely in the creature is not in the least degree comparable to his comeliness, she takes fire and burns toward that invisible fire, and, experiencing the wound of charity inflicted upon her mind by the sweet sting of the Godhead, and demanding that there be foretasted for her certain pledges, as it were, both of the blessedness to come and of that most sacred conjunction of the created spirit with the uncreated, which shall be without end in an indissoluble bond of charity, with an inward; and crying out with a sound of the mind audible to the holy and supernal powers alone, she says, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. » For love kindled toward God is charity; and [1154D] the beholding, with intent mind, of him who is loved is contemplation: and these so accompany one another that contemplation stirs up love, and love always advances contemplation toward the things before; so that whither contemplation penetrates by the ray of the supernal light, thither it draws love after it; so that to the soul thus advancing the Lord is both illumination through contemplation, and true salvation through charity; as it is said, « The Lord is my illumination, and my salvation; whom shall I fear? » [n: (Psal. XXVI, 1.)] The soul, therefore, turned away from the world and converted to Christ with her whole mind, forgetting the things that are behind [n: (Phil. III, 13)], and stretching herself mightily toward the things before, beholding the world now far down beneath her, snatching herself wholly into eternity, [1155A] beholding by contemplation the highest and eternal things of the Lord Jesus, and by urgent love desiring them, because she wholly succumbs to love and languishes with spiritual desire; yet not presuming upon the full embraces of the bridegroom, that her love may be satisfied at least in something, asks a kiss, and, speaking in mind either to herself or perhaps to a familiar angel, imparting spiritual things to the spiritual, opens her love, and, loving, so begins from love, saying, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. » And since these things have been said in the manner of a little preface, we shall expound the rest in the following tome, the Lord breathing upon us, who lives and reigns for all ages of ages. Amen.

*Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.*

By unremitting labour, by continual exercise of virtue, this faithful [1155B] soul has been brought so far that she aspires to the kiss of the highest King, saying, « Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. » Hence it is that we by no means run on with a gliding pen, but stand as though clinging upon the heights, desiring earnestly to search out and to imitate the things at once hidden and perfect of this holy soul. In which matter this first occurs, that she seems most confidently to glory in herself together with the Apostle, so as to say, « Our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience [n: (II Cor. I, 12)]. » For she who seeks the kiss of the highest Godhead knows beyond doubt that she has a clean heart, knows that she has clean lips, an honourable face, and one not unworthy of the kiss of so great a King: so that there seems rightly to belong to her what was said, « For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you a chaste virgin [1155C] to a chaste one [n: (II Cor. XI, 2)]: » [var: Vulg. *Christo*, "to Christ"] and again elsewhere, « That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot, nor wrinkle [n: (Ephes. V, 27)]: » for this soul has no « spot » from uncleanness, no « wrinkle » from duplicity, no depraved conscience from hatred of a neighbour; there proceed from her heart no murders, no adulteries, none of the other things that are wont to weigh down the conscience and are wont to defile a man: for with all watchfulness she keeps her own heart, hearing attentively through Solomon, « for from it life proceedeth. [n: (Prov. IV, 23)]. » At the doors of this heart stands the fear of God, provident and solicitous, lest on every side a way of approach to its secret places lie open to the vices: at the bulwarks of this heart stand the stern battalions of the virtues, which do not now, as of late, fight against sins; [1155D] but glory in the Lord Jesus, the victory over them being even now obtained: and by how much the bitterer the battle they long experienced, by so much the more joyful is the glory in which they now triumph. Above stands chastity girt up, which rejoices that she has crushed the uncleanness of the flesh upon the rock of abstinence. With placid countenance stands humility, the companion of chastity, minding nothing lofty; but repressing by the Lord's power the elation of mind that ever seeks high things, and bravely and prudently dashing the foul madness of its head against the rock, which is Christ. Thus faith despises unbelief, hope despairing misery, charity envy, simplicity guile, innocence malice, truth falsehood, and each several virtue despises the vices opposed to it, as [1156A] monstrous corpses now mightily dashed against the rock of truth. Here thou mayest see that ancient concupiscence of the flesh lamenting at the funerals of her extinguished offspring; carrying round in the golden cup of Babylon her various allurements, and all that can be contrived by the most exquisite art of temptation, plotting this by force, this by all her craft, to see whether the things grown cold may be warmed, and the things extinguished may be raised up to their ancient spirit of life. That sacred choir of the virtues mocks her as she casts her darts, knowing that the Egyptians, smitten by the hand of the Lord, are not to be called back to life any more: whence, exulting spiritually, it takes up psalm and timbrel, singing out that song of Moses with full gladness to the Lord, « Let us sing to the Lord; for he is gloriously magnified: the horse and the rider he hath cast into [1156B] the sea [n: (Exod. XV, 1)]. » The evil rider is every malignant spirit; the evil horses are the worst vices; and with what violence the evil Angels who sit upon them are borne along is manifest, when they drag down souls wretchedly tempted into the depth of hell, and subject them to eternal torments, the divine justice bringing it about.



## CHAPTER ONE. (cont.)

This soul glories that these are extinguished for her, and, sitting in the midst of the virtues, now entrusts herself wholly to them, and commits herself utterly to their services; and to her every virtue does service most humbly, each furnishing what is its own. Who could now run through with the pen, who could set forth in speech, what comeliness each several virtue confers upon this perfect soul, what admirable grace each several virtue supplies? Who could express her comeliness to the full? whom [1156C] continence renders chaste, and innocence simple, meekness gentle, mercy devout, circumspection provident, temperance sober, prudence discreet, patience brave; and whom charity, now perfected, directs with much reverence along the sacred paths of justice? For from the very beginning of holy fear, straightway planting her steps in humility, thence passing through the camps of unchastity, and so ascending through the remaining virtues as they are disposed in the mind by the Spirit of God, looking no longer upon vanities and false madnesses, she now entrusts herself wholly to love in a certain higher place, and commits herself to its most excellent fullness. Here, dwelling apart, she cannot but meditate upon what she loves; she cannot but contemplate [1156D] what she desires: with a thirst sent upon her from above, she takes fire toward that living fountain, and is daily refreshed with the sweet bread of tears; while she grieves that her desires are drawn out to such length, and, suffused with tears, makes her complaint. Here she frequently repeats and turns over with herself that saying, « To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain: I desire to be dissolved, and to be with Christ [n: (Phil. I, 21, 23)]. » And that other, « Woe is me! that my sojourning is prolonged [n: (Psal. CXIX, 5)]. » She is indeed forced to feel, and compelled to experience in herself, what she lacks of the highest, and how far off she is from eternity. A spirit released from the flesh has seen manifestly him whom it loves, enjoys the good it desires, is not tormented by the deferring of its desire, is touched by no grief at all; there love is wholly in the light, wholly rests in joy: [1157A] but the weariness of love in the present life is beautifully described, when it is said, « Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning taketh hold of the ends of joy [n: (Prov. XIV, 13)]. »

In this life indeed the laughter of a faithful soul is this: that with a clean conscience, with a perfect heart, with a most full integrity of love, she knows that she follows the Lord Jesus into the heights, and that she reaches out the kiss of her mind toward his human things and his divine alike: yet this laughter is still mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes hold of this joy; since she knows that she has not yet apprehended him whom she follows with her heart, and considers that what she desires above all things is deferred from her.
